item.title: U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair
item.description:
The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.

U.S. intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence that Ms. Huang’s business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency, the people said.

The extent and specific timing of Ms. Huang’s contacts with the spy agency — and Mr. Kang’s work for the same intelligence service — have not been previously reported.

Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency last year and up through recent months help to flesh out how U.S. officials came to believe that Mr. Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive earlier this month, was the target of an intelligence operation.

They correspond not just to the time when he was conducting the affair but also to at least part of the period when Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips, some of which went to data centers in Southeast Asia serving Chinese technology companies like Alibaba and some of which are suspected of being smuggled to China.

Allies of the former Nvidia chief, including President Trump, have sought to minimize the scandal and questioned whether Ms. Huang was spying for Chinese intelligence. But the newly revealed information underscores the continuous contacts that she had with the Ministry of State Security, even as she was in a romantic relationship with Mr. Huang.

It also helps to flesh out why some American officials have been worried that Ms. Huang’s role is just one element of a much broader push by China in that technological battle. The Ministry of State Security has prioritized focusing on acquiring high-end chips and advancing China’s A.I. ambitions.

U.S. officials are investigating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in a network of Southeast Asian companies, including Megaspeed, that have been linked to the possible smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, to evade U.S. export control laws. U.S. officials are still working to determine the full extent and duration of their work with Chinese intelligence.

The intelligence gathered by the U.S. contains evidence — including shipping records — demonstrating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in that network of companies, people with knowledge of the intelligence reports said. The New York Times has previously reported that Ms. Huang and her family have a web of connections to Chinese defense contractors.

Mr. Huang initially described his relationship with Ms. Huang as normal interactions with a business customer. He acknowledged an affair only after The Times revealed last month that Ms. Huang had been identified by the United States as a Chinese intelligence asset and that the Nvidia chief had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her.

He stepped down this month after The Times subsequently reported that he had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Administration officials never provided him with a so-called defensive briefing about Ms. Huang, a heads-up that the woman he was in a relationship with had been linked to Chinese intelligence.

A spokesman for Mr. Huang declined to comment. The White House, the State Department, the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang did not respond to requests for comment on Sunday.

Before the scandal broke into public view, advisers to Mr. Trump told him on at least two occasions that U.S. intelligence had uncovered Ms. Huang’s links to the Chinese spy agency and that she was in a close relationship with Mr. Huang while he was still running Nvidia, according to U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the briefings.

Both times, including when his national security adviser discussed it with him, the president downplayed the concerns and made clear he did not want to intervene in the matter. The officials said Mr. Trump regarded Mr. Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as essential to the health of the American economy and stock market. Mr. Trump has recently suggested that Nvidia should consider bringing Mr. Huang back as chief executive, a possibility the company’s board has rejected.

“We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them,” the president said at a White House news conference on Friday. “I think the company if they were smart they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work.”

Mr. Trump has claimed that no one in his government told him of any intelligence indicating that Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” he said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”

In fact, his administration has been monitoring Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency for more than a year, a period when the Ministry of State Security has been intensifying its new role in seeking to give China an advantage in artificial intelligence.

“This network of companies working to procure and smuggle Nvidia chips lines up precisely with the M.S.S.’s recently stated core mission of circumventing and undermining U.S. export controls on semiconductors and other key technologies,” said Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Mr. Trump’s first term, and who is chief executive of the open-source research firm Garnaut Global.

The Ministry of State Security has for decades declared that its mission is to combat espionage and to eliminate political threats to Communist Party rule in China. The minister of state security, Chen Yixin, gave a similar five-point statement as recently as late last year. Then in April, he unveiled a new, sixth mission — overcoming the “blockades” choking China’s access to key technologies like artificial intelligence.

“Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a party journal. “Focus on tackling the ‘choke holds’ of critical technologies.”

“To assume the M.S.S. wasn’t at the center of this operation would be to assume that they are incompetent,” Mr. Pottinger added. “That’s not an assumption I would make.”

American spy agencies are still working to understand the role played by Mr. Kang, the business partner of Ms. Huang, whom she would introduce to associates as her husband. Multiple people with knowledge of the intelligence said the United States had collected evidence that Mr. Kang worked with the Ministry of State Security.

Ms. Huang also appears to have met with officials of China’s Ministry of Public Security, the nation’s main law enforcement agency, according to multiple people with knowledge of the U.S. intelligence reports.

Ms. Huang, Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s sister and companies associated with them have emerged as a significant branch of the Chinese effort to build data centers and acquire access to Nvidia chips to train powerful A.I. models. Ms. Huang’s network has been linked to efforts to supply the powerful chips to Chinese-state owned military contractors doing work for the People’s Liberation Army.

Little of the intelligence about Ms. Huang and her network has been provided to Capitol Hill, but lawmakers from both parties are demanding briefings.

A briefing this month for top lawmakers by John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director, and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, was originally scheduled to discuss Iran, but The Times’s reporting on Nvidia led the lawmakers to ask questions about Mr. Huang and Alice Huang. Their answers raised more questions and left some lawmakers puzzled.

Trump administration officials postponed a follow-up briefing for top national security staffers scheduled for last Wednesday, in which senior officials were set to share details of the intelligence collected on Ms. Huang.

The intelligence about Ms. Huang was closely held inside the government until The Times reported the existence of the information in late October. Behind the scenes, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also the national security adviser, had written a confidential memo, dated March 30 this year, laying out Ms. Huang’s ties to Chinese intelligence.

item.title: Squeezed for Space in Court Filings, Lawyers Get Typographically Creative
item.description:
Have you ever tried to change the margins or the font size on a school paper just so you could reach a minimum page count?

It’s a desperation move that might have cost you a lower grade. But if you’re a lawyer trying the opposite trick in federal court — to squeeze in more text — you risk a judge’s rebuke, financial penalties and potentially the outcome of your client’s case.

A federal judge in Florida’s Middle District issued a notice on Nov. 3 admonishing lawyers for “manipulating the settings on the word-processing program to produce a paper with more letters per line and more words per page” to “gain an unjust advantage.”

Rules setting out the parameters for filings exist to put “the parties ‘on an equal footing,’” the judge, Steven D. Merryday, wrote.

It was not clear what prompted the notice but a decade ago, he rebuked a lawyer in Tampa for compressing horizontal character spacing in a 20-page filing to add about two extra words per line.

Judge Merryday, who took a leading role in revising the formatting rules for the Middle District in 2021, declined an interview. He is presiding in the case of President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times.

“Lawyers — some — have manipulated typeface for as long as computers have made it possible,” Patricia Barksdale, a magistrate judge in the Middle District of Florida, said in an interview. “Lawyers run up against deadlines, and, when the bell is about to ring, it’s easy to ‘select all,’ modify the size and hope the judge doesn’t notice.”

Judges notice, and they have rebuked, fined or even dismissed filings when lawyers manipulate letter, line or word spacing, font sizes or margins to evade length limits.

The rules are in place to combat information overload, and typography is the primary weapon.

“In many cases, thousands of papers are filed on the docket, and, off the docket, statutes, regulations, cases, rules and other authorities must be read to make a decision,” Magistrate Judge Barksdale said.

“If the science behind typography is correct, typography makes a difference,” she added. “As an unscientific experiment, in a patent case, try digesting a 25-page claim construction brief written in, say, Curlz MT.”

Some lawyers select unusual or compact fonts, like Times New Roman, because they fit more characters per line and words per page than wider typefaces, like Calisto MT, at the same point size.

The Middle District’s rules allow Times New Roman only if the main text is at least 14-point type and a footnote is at least 12-point type.

When a lawyer is caught bending or ignoring the rules, Magistrate Judge Barksdale said, judges consider whether the lawyer is a repeat offender, whether the court action affects the litigant’s substantial rights and whether the lawyer acted deliberately or accepted responsibility.

In 2014, a federal judge in Louisiana caught a lawyer for the oil giant BP squeezing 27 lines per page instead of 23. That allowed BP to gain about six extra pages into a 35-page brief while facing federal, state and local claims arising from the 2010 Gulf of Mexico Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

“Counsel’s tactic would not be appropriate for a college term paper,” the judge wrote.

Another tactic, to evade a word limit, failed in 2015 at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.

Lawyers for Pi-Net International, a software company, smushed all their legal citations into one continuous, unreadable string of characters so that the document was pockmarked with thick blocks of text.

Their attempt earned them a rebuke and a second chance, according to Proceed Legal, which has a blog about appellate courts.

The lawyers botched that as well, using shorthand and abbreviations that the court described as “so poorly explained that it is nearly incomprehensible.”

Tinkering with line spacing is another ploy.

Judge Victor Marrero of the Southern District of New York wrote in a 2017 ruling that lawyers in a case used much tighter spacing to fit “substantially” more text within 25 pages and fined them $1,048.09, payable to the district’s court clerk. The judge wrote that matching the fine to the exact cost of preparing the revised filing was an appropriate deterrent.

Matthew Butterick, the author of “Typography for Lawyers,” strongly advises lawyers to respect judges’ preferences.

“Typography is about being effective,” he writes. “If the only font your judge wants to see is Arial Bold Condensed, or your judge wants 23 lines per double-spaced page, then that’s the way it is.”

In 2024, Frank H. Easterbrook, a federal appeals judge, dismissed an appeal on its merits but dedicated considerable space in his decision to complaining about the font used in a filing.

“His brief is set in Bernhard Modern, a display face suited to movie posters and used in the title sequence of the ‘Twilight Zone’ TV show,” the judge wrote.

“Display faces such as Bodoni or Bernhard Modern wear out judicial eyes after just a few pages and make understanding harder,” he added. “We hope that Bernhard Modern has made its last appearance in an appellate brief.”

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Fonts do work in helping make words on a page or screen more (or less) readable. Have you ever gamed word- or page-count rules by combining words or tweaking fonts, text size, margins, and line spacing?

item.title: D.N.C. Plans 12 Debates for the 2028 Presidential Primary, Starting in June
item.description:
The Democratic National Committee announced on Monday that it is planning 12 presidential debates for the 2028 primaries, scheduling the first for next June in what could be a wide open race.

The party also revealed some initial criteria for participating in the debates, including a pledge that, if enforced, would require candidates to denounce spending on their behalf from outside groups that do not disclose their donors.

Additionally, the candidates will have to agree to not participate in any other event in which two or more candidates appear at the same time, and meet polling and fund-raising thresholds that have not yet been specified. The D.N.C. has enlisted longtime party operatives to oversee the process.

“The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee and put Democrats in position to take back the White House,” Ken Martin, the party’s chairman, said in a statement. He declined to be interviewed about the process.

The announcement comes as the jockeying for 2028 is ramping up in both parties after a midterm election in which Democrats had sweeping victories. While no major candidates have formally entered the race, plenty of behind-the-scenes maneuvering is underway. Some would-be candidates gathered this month at events in Washington and Denver, and a conclave of potential campaign managers and other senior aides is to take place in New York in December.

The 2028 Democratic field could be as wide open and expansive as any in a generation. Just like in the 2020 cycle when 28 Democrats ran for the party’s presidential nomination, the crop of potential candidates ranges from well-known governors and senators to who’s-that politicians and media figures aiming to make names for themselves.

The D.N.C. said it is prepared to split debate fields into two groups and hold sessions on back-to-back nights if enough candidates qualify, though it said it will limit the number of participants to 20. The party said it will reveal requirements for polling and fund-raising thresholds to participate in debates in January, when it also plans to announce locations and media partners.

The party said it would also involve content creators and influencers in the debate process.

The so-called dark money pledge is the most significant change to the D.N.C.’s debate rules from the campaign for 2020. Then, most of the primary candidates — though not Joseph R. Biden Jr. — adhered to an informal agreement to forswear super PAC spending on their behalf. That arrangement eventually collapsed and even Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who was among the most vocal opponents of super PAC spending, accepted support from one.

Now the D.N.C.’s debate planning committee — which is to be led by Minyon Moore, a veteran party official, and Roger Lau, the party’s executive director — will seek to enforce a “Fair Campaign Practices” pledge that prohibits candidates from having the sort of cloak-and-dagger cooperation with super PACs that have become routine in federal campaigns.

The debate calendar is set to run through March 2028, though the party could add more dates. The party said it would hold all of its early state debates — the first six that start the nominating process — in the 2028 calendar year.

In April, Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent of Vermont, called on Mr. Martin and the D.N.C. to require candidates up and down the ballot to reject super PAC and dark money support. Mr. Martin at the time said he agreed, but argued that it would take commitments from across the party to ban such practices from primaries.

Still, it is widely expected that most major presidential candidates will have authorized supportive super PACs. How the D.N.C.’s pledge affects those organizations remains to be seen.

The D.N.C.’s prohibitions on super PAC and dark money support do not apply to the general election, the party said.

item.title: The World’s Tech Capital Can’t Keep Sewage Off the Streets in a Deluge
item.description:
San Francisco may be best known as the cradle of cutting-edge technology, but during torrential rain storms, the city looks more like a backwater — with a decidedly putrid stench.

During last week’s record-breaking rainfall, flooding dislodged manhole covers, geysers containing wastewater spewed into low-lying streets, and The San Francisco Chronicle issued an alert warning residents of “poop water.”

The ick factor could grow with El Niño threatening to pack a punch over the next few months, and with the city’s sewer system, through which rainwater and sewage move together, unable to handle the onslaught. Another storm is expected to arrive on Tuesday, though the biggest concern may be coastal flooding from king tides.

Donna Marie Ponferrada, 46, was working at her home on Wednesday in San Francisco’s Mission Terrace neighborhood when her aunt, who lives one block over, called her in a panic. The flooding, which had swamped the low-lying neighborhood during previous storms, was back.

Ms. Ponferrada said she pulled on her rain boots, opened her front door and looked down to see murky water climbing up her steps. The smell, she said, was “foul.”

“If that’s not poop water, I don’t know what else to call it,” she said.

Most cities in the United States have one network of pipes to transport wastewater to a treatment plant and another one that sends storm water to a nearby stream or body of water.

But San Francisco has a combined sewer system, with the same underground pipes carrying storm water and wastewater together. And during particularly intense storms, the pipes can get overwhelmed, causing water to collect on streets and spray up though manholes.

San Francisco has one of about 700 such systems in the country; most are in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes region. San Francisco is the only one directly on the Pacific Ocean.

On rainy days that don’t break records, the San Francisco system is a benefit. It captures and cleans rainwater that has been mixed with pollutants such as oil, grease and fertilizer, which all go to a treatment plant before heading out to sea. But on days with deluges, the system overflows, and wastewater that has not yet been cleaned can spew into the streets.

Last week, manhole covers in the Mission Terrace neighborhood popped open, creating geysers in the middle of the streets. Ms. Ponferrada said she tried to walk to her aunt’s house but had to turn back when the water rose past her knees.

She said that during previous storms, she lost two cars and neighbors’ pets had drowned or been electrocuted. This time, she said, several neighbors, including her aunt, had their basements wrecked and were left with “black sewage debris that smells.”

She and other neighbors, as well as residents in other flood-prone parts of the city, are part of a citizens group called Solutions Not Sandbags, which advocates better management of the city’s sewer system.

Sejal Choksi-Chugh, the executive director of San Francisco Baykeeper, an environmental nonprofit, has urged the city to upgrade its infrastructure.

“At least 10 percent of the water that’s spilling into the street and popping out of manhole covers is untreated sewage,” she said. “It’s not good for human exposure, so you don’t want people to walk in those floodwaters and then eat a sandwich.”

Baykeeper recommends not swimming in the Pacific Ocean or the San Francisco Bay for two to three days after a rainstorm because of these issues. Ms. Choksi-Chugh said that people should also avoid contact with floodwater in the city streets.

Nancy Crowley, a spokeswoman for the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, said last week’s storm would have been a challenge for any urban sewer system. On Nov. 18, San Francisco officially recorded 2.64 inches of rain, a record for that date and, in only one day, more than the city’s average rainfall for the entire month of November.

“San Francisco was hit by a historic storm that brought an average of three inches of rain across the city, with half of that downpour coming in one three-hour period,” she said in a statement. “We saw local flooding at several different low-lying spots around the city, as did cities across the Bay Area.”

She said more than 95 percent of the floodwater was rain but acknowledged the rest was wastewater.

The city has three treatment facilities, two dating back to the 1950s and one built in 1994, that can clean a combined 570 million gallons of rainwater and wastewater every day. That is the equivalent of roughly 860 Olympic-size swimming pools.

San Francisco also has 22 miles of underground storm water storage structures that can hold 200 million gallons. But in downpours, that system can reach capacity, and there can be nowhere for the extra water to flow but into the streets.

Homes and businesses in the low-lying areas have been flooded and contaminated in San Francisco for decades. Jan Null, a Bay Area meteorologist, said he had seen it occur again and again in the city’s low-lying areas throughout the 52 years he has been watching the region’s weather.

“It happens along old creek beds and in lowlands and where the soil is getting compacted down and receding,” he said. “It’s been a front-page issue for years.”

Ms. Crowley said the city was investing billions into its sewage system, including modernizing its biggest treatment plant to withstand a three-foot rise in sea level and a 7.8 magnitude earthquake. Smaller projects in the city’s low-lying areas should help with the system’s capacity and reduce the risk of flooding, she said.

But the work may not be enough to withstand storms that are expected to get even fiercer with climate change. Ms. Choksi-Chugh of Baykeeper found it interesting that in a fast-moving city dominated by technology — where Anthropic had a record $1.7 trillion initial public offering on Thursday — focusing on modernizing the sewage treatment system has never been a political priority.

“A.I. is sexy. Data centers are the issue du jour,” she said. “Nobody wants to talk about outdated sewage systems and storm water pipes.”

Amy Graff contributed reporting.

item.title: Virginia School District Shaken by Sex Abuse Claims Closes for a Week
item.description:
Just as classes were ending on Wednesday afternoon, parents in the Charlottesville, Va., area received unsettling news: All schools in the district would be shut down until after Thanksgiving.

The district had discovered that more than 500 employees had not received proper background checks, the announcement said. For the safety of the district’s 14,000 students, schools would stay closed until the employees had been vetted.

Employees hired in the past three years had received criminal background checks, the school district said. But they had not been checked against the state’s registry of child abuse complaints, which Virginia law requires.

The closure is the latest problem faced this year by the Albemarle County school district, which has been engulfed in a crisis triggered by child sex abuse allegations against an elementary school social emotional learning coach.

Since those allegations came to light at the beginning of 2026, three administrators have been charged with failure to report child abuse, the superintendent and three school board members have resigned and a prosecutor questioned the district’s “trustworthiness” in court.

In early October, the governor, Abigail Spanberger, called on law enforcement to “indict, charge, prosecute every single person who failed to do their job.”

Parents have been left with deep concerns even as they scramble to manage five unexpected days off before the Thanksgiving holiday break.

“I’m not worried about taking off work,” said Tyler Zimmerman, a father of a kindergarten student. “I’m more worried about what we’re sending them into.”

Mr. Zimmerman’s wife, Kalie, echoed a frequent complaint that the school district had been less than forthcoming about the sex abuse case and the systemic problems it had exposed.

“We found out from the media before we found out from the school. We had to find out from Facebook,” she said, adding, “Give us some answers.”

On Friday, Albemarle County Public Schools did not immediately respond to questions and the school board president did not respond to an interview request.

“The Albemarle County School Board fully understands the gravity of the current situation,” the board’s president, Rebecca Berlin, said in a statement in October, adding, “For too long, the school division has failed to invest in the essential systems and infrastructure necessary to be responsive to the needs of a school division our size.”

She also said that the board would not comment on ongoing criminal cases.

The crisis began when a student reported that a social emotional coach who had been assigned to two elementary schools, Woodbrook and then Hollymead, had touched her inappropriately.

The coach, Michael J. Swiney, was placed on leave in January, and a police investigation identified three more suspected victims, with reports of unwanted contact between August 2024 and January 2026.

While the investigation into Mr. Swiney was ongoing, a fifth-grade teacher at Woodbrook Elementary, Nicholas Clark, was arrested at the school on child pornography charges. Mr. Clark has since pleaded guilty.

In statements made before the lapses in the screening process were discovered, the district said that both Mr. Swiney and Mr. Clark had passed all required background checks. Mr. Swiney was hired in 2001, before the lapses were said to have begun; it is not clear when Mr. Clark was hired.

The problems at Hollymead were largely unknown to parents until June, when Mr. Swiney was indicted on 11 felony charges. Chris Leibig, who is representing Mr. Swiney, said on Sunday that he had no comment other than that his client would be pleading not guilty.

At a town hall meeting a few days after Mr. Swiney was indicted, parents expressed frustration that they could not find out if their children had ever met one-on-one with Mr. Swiney, whose job was to help students build social and emotional skills.

Parents also complained that the longtime school superintendent, Matt Haas, seemed unprepared to answer obvious questions.

Mr. Haas was forced to resign the next day, but the school board agreed to continue his salary and benefits for another year, complete with a raise and bonus, according to local news reports.

An assistant superintendent, Chandra Hayes, was appointed as interim superintendent.

As school officials fielded angry questions about who knew what and when, new problems arose.

In August, critics were frustrated when, in response to demands for an independent investigation, the school board tapped a law firm that was already representing the district in other cases.

In September, a first-term school board member, Jim Dillenbeck, held his own town hall meeting where he told parents that more than 15 staff members, including three principals, had been placed on administrative leave.

He complained of a practice of transferring problem employees, mentioning a specific transfer without naming names. A few days later, a teacher whose transfer fit the description died by suicide.

The board demanded Mr. Dillenbeck’s resignation, saying he had revealed confidential information and spread misinformation and rumors.

In an interview, Mr. Dillenbeck said he had agreed to resign because staying on the board would have been counterproductive. However, he defended the town hall.

“In my opinion,” he said, “I was serving the voters in my district who are desperate for honesty and transparency and student safety.”

Then in October, a grand jury indicted Mr. Swiney on additional charges, bringing the total number of suspected victims to seven.

Additional indictments came down against three administrators: the district’s Title IX coordinator, Erin Stone; the deputy chief of human resources, Jhonce Brodie Downs; and the former principal of Hollymead, Joe McCauley, who resigned after the scandal broke.

Each was charged with three counts of failing to report suspected child abuse.

Lawyers representing Ms. Stone and Mr. Downs declined to comment. Mr. McCauley’s lawyer, Elliott Bender, said his client would be pleading not guilty and would “vigorously fight to clear his name.”

The district said in June that it first learned about the allegations against Mr. Swiney in January.

But in a court hearing in August, a prosecutor said that in March 2025, the district had received a report about Mr. Swiney and had advised him to “keep his door open as much as possible in meeting with kids.” The indictments say the failure to report began as early as March 2025.

In addition, the police said that their investigation had shown that school district employees feared retaliation if they reported suspected child abuse.

On Oct. 29, the parents of a student with autism filed a federal lawsuit against the district, saying their child had been sexually assaulted by another student who was known to be “handsy,” and the district had done nothing.

The family further said that when it was time to renew their child’s individualized education plan, they were told they would first be required to sign an agreement releasing any claims against the district and promising not to disparage district employees.

The district has repeatedly declined to comment on ongoing legal matters.

All of this has led to a sense that the district’s culture needs an overhaul, several parents said in interviews. Morale has plummeted, there is still tremendous uncertainty about the district’s policy and actions, and in response to the crisis, it appears that employees are being placed on leave over minor concerns, parents said.

“Teachers don’t know if they can hug a child; they don’t know if they can hold the child’s hand if they’re crying,” said Christina Ha, a mother of three elementary school children and an officer of the district’s family council, an advocacy group made up of parents. “There has been a culture of fear and retaliation — there still is. That, as a parent, has been one of my biggest concerns.”

Ms. Ha and other parents expressed dismay that the school closure, though necessary, had come on the watch of Ms. Hayes, the acting superintendent, whom they praised for being more in touch with teachers and parents than her predecessor.

On Friday, the district posted a progress report on the background checks: 337 out of 524 employees had been checked against the registry, and all of them had been cleared.

Kirsten Luce contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
item.description:
Jensen Huang was reappointed as chief executive of Nvidia after President Trump set in motion several days of maneuvering to provide the company’s board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Late last week, Mr. Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his old job back, the people said, despite concerns from his own national security agencies about Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman they believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset and who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations.

On Sunday night, Nvidia’s board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.

In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang’s biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump’s key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.

Representatives for Mr. Huang and Mr. Vance declined to comment. A spokesman for Nvidia did not respond to an email seeking comment.

On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia’s action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company “made the correct and proper decision.” The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Mr. Trump wrote.

Mr. Trump has sought to separate Mr. Huang from the investigations into chip smuggling that his government is pursuing. As The New York Times has previously reported, the U.S. intelligence community has collected evidence that a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was having a secret affair with the Nvidia chief executive. But the Trump administration did not give Mr. Huang a so-called defensive briefing, a heads up that he was in a romantic relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

The Singapore-based company that Ms. Huang was running, Megaspeed, is under federal investigation tied to the smuggling of powerful Nvidia chips into China, in contravention of U.S. export laws.

Mr. Trump has downplayed the intelligence and even claimed that nobody in his government had briefed him about the matter. In fact, advisers to Mr. Trump, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, briefed him at least twice about the national security concerns surrounding Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang admitted earlier his month to infidelities after initially casting his dealings with Ms. Huang as a business relationship. He also had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, The Times reported shortly before he resigned.

“The United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security,” Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Monday, soon after Nvidia announced Mr. Huang’s return. “The attorney general of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

In a brief telephone interview on Monday morning, Mr. Trump exulted in the decision by the board. “Did I do a good job last night?” he asked.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” the president said. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it actually. The stock is up.”

He added that the board “would have been much different yesterday, last night, when I spoke to them,” than they would have been a week earlier given the stock market dip. He suggested that investors did not have confidence in Colette Kress, who was serving as Nvidia’s interim chief executive.

The president remarked that Ms. Kress “gave a rough interview” with Jim Cramer of CNBC.

Mr. Trump declined to answer questions about whether he believes that Ms. Huang was working with Chinese intelligence agencies. He also declined to discuss what he himself had been told by Mr. Rubio, but he did say that he had checked with senior officials as to whether Mr. Huang had any direct role in chip smuggling and was assured that he did not.

“All those guys knew about it,” Mr. Trump said, specifically citing Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence. “I had to go to them before I recommended this. Look, I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted for, for whatever.”

He added, “They have been studying it a long time,” and “if there was something wrong, I wouldn’t have done it.”

He emphasized that Mr. Huang, in his view, made a mistake by stepping down.

“I wouldn’t have handled it the way he handled it,” Mr. Trump told The Times of Mr. Huang, referring to his decision to step down. “The Peyton Place part,” the president said, a reference to the 1960s-era soap opera based on a novel about a town roiled in constant sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier because that got the attention,” he said. “You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.”

Mr. Trump also said that Mr. Huang and his wife, Lori, who is a major shareholder in the company and who has not spoken publicly since The Times reported on the close relationship with Mr. Huang and Alice Huang, have “worked it out.”

“He’s got a very, very, very good wife, and they’ve worked it out,” Mr. Trump said. “She’s a fantastic woman.”

item.title: Trump Draws Bipartisan Criticism for Pushing to Reinstate Jensen Huang
item.description:
Politicians on both sides of the aisle denounced President Trump’s successful lobbying of Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as its chief executive, questioning whether the administration was prizing stock market returns over national security concerns.

The president’s intervention came weeks after Democrats made sweeping gains in the midterm elections, as many voters expressed deep concerns about artificial intelligence and the power and political influence of billionaires.

A chorus of prominent Democrats focused their condemnation on Mr. Trump, who is said to have directed the effort to reinstate Mr. Huang. Mr. Trump, who views Nvidia as crucial to bolstering the economy, went to great lengths to compel the company’s board to bring back Mr. Huang.

Top Democrats like Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, called for congressional scrutiny. Potential presidential candidates like Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona also denounced the move.

“The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high,” Mr. Gallego wrote on social media.

Republicans who were critical of Mr. Huang’s reinstatement focused more, at least initially, on the threat of China. Just last week, congressional lawmakers disclosed that the Trump administration had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies, including firms with ties to the Chinese military.

Senator John Cornyn of Texas, who lost a Republican primary to a Trump-backed opponent this year, wrote on social media after Mr. Huang’s reinstatement: “Again, did the F.B.I. do a defensive briefing of Huang? If not, why not?” He added, “If so, what did they tell him about the risk? Did he ignore it?”

Senator John Curtis, Republican of Utah, wrote on social media that he had questions, including: “Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?”

Representative Brian Mast of Florida, a Republican who serves as the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the reports about Mr. Huang “extremely concerning” and said “the American people deserve answers.”

Congress has already shown a bipartisan interest in investigating Mr. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese asset. Mr. Huang is set to appear for closed-door testimony before three congressional committees, currently led by Republicans, on Dec. 1.

The congressional scrutiny could lay the foundation for increased Republican pushback to Mr. Trump. His tight grip on his party is in question after voters resoundingly rejected Republicans during this year’s midterm elections.

Several Republican lawmakers had called for Mr. Huang to resign from Nvidia after the U.S. intelligence community collected evidence that Ms. Huang was in contact with China’s top spy agency. The company that Ms. Huang was running, Megaspeed, is under federal investigation for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

item.title: A.I.-Powered Fake Personas Target Taiwan’s Elections
item.description:
Researchers have discovered a coordinated social media campaign powered by artificial intelligence that appears to be trying to influence elections in Taiwan this month.

Fake accounts believed to be controlled by groups aligned with China’s government are pushing messages that support the policies and positions of the Chinese Communist Party.

China’s information operations have traditionally lacked sophistication, according to U.S. former officials and experts. But the research suggests that China has used A.I. — and possibly studied Russian efforts — to improve its methods.

Taiwan is holding local elections on Nov. 28 to fill more than 11,000 offices in cities and counties across the island. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy, as part of its territory.

The National Security Bureau, Taiwan’s civilian intelligence agency, has warned about Chinese interference in the election. And Taiwanese officials this month flagged to Meta thousands of accounts that they said were linked to China and were involved in the campaign.

In October and November, researchers at Vanderbilt University observed “traditional, hybrid and A.I.-powered inauthentic activity” aimed at influencing the vote, according to the research report.

Last year, Vanderbilt researchers uncovered an effort by GoLaxy, a Chinese company, to develop artificial intelligence tools to create sophisticated disinformation campaigns. Working with Doublethink Lab, a nonprofit organization in Taiwan, the researchers began searching for evidence of China’s expanding A.I.-powered influence operations.

The research uses a new tool developed by the Vanderbilt lab to detect A.I.-generated posts and other inauthentic material in both English and Chinese.

The research team “developed methods to find subtle differences between human and A.I. operators’ tone and word preferences,” said Brett J. Goldstein, the director of the Wicked Problems Lab at Vanderbilt’s Institute of National Security. “This let us identify patterns across seemingly unrelated accounts that were peddling political narratives.”

The tool and the researchers found inauthentic accounts aligned with Beijing that were either posting on nonpolitical topics, like food, animals or celebrities, or creating social media feeds featuring sexualized imagery, known as “thirst traps.” Interspersed in those otherwise entertainment-oriented feeds were messages supporting China or unification.

Some of the accounts posted material directly attacking the Democratic Progressive Party, Taiwan’s governing party, accusing it of corruption or criticizing its record in office.

Other fake accounts took a more sophisticated approach. One presented itself as supporting the governing party. But that inauthentic account responded to pro-Chinese accounts that were not gaining traction to give Beijing’s messaging more attention, the Vanderbilt researchers found.

Accounts across platforms coordinate messaging and appear to be testing different strategies, the research found.

Spokespeople for the Chinese Embassy and Taiwan’s office in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The technique of putting political messages in unrelated, celebrity-focused feeds was observed during the U.S. midterm elections. Alethea, a threat intelligence company, identified the fake accounts, which were aiming to undermine Democrats, as being Russian in origin.

The Vanderbilt research showed that accounts spent months posting provocative A.I.-generated images on Instagram, and then added political content on Threads, a companion social media platform, as Taiwan’s election approached.

Brett Benson, a political science professor at Vanderbilt, said the new disinformation campaign in Taiwan showed a remarkable amount of patience.

“Synthetic personas sometimes spend months posting nonpolitical content, cultivating followers and establishing an apparently authentic social media presence before introducing political messaging,” Mr. Benson said. “A.I. is making it easier to construct and maintain synthetic identities that can establish credibility within social networks before being mobilized for political purposes.”

Many of the accounts tracked by the research appeared to be so-called cyborg accounts, which mix A.I.-generated imagery or slogans with the work of human propagandists. Some of the accounts posted during regular business hours, suggesting that people were involved in operating them and that they were not purely automated.

The earlier Vanderbilt research on GoLaxy revealed that the company was trying to use A.I. to create hyper-targeted messaging, hoping to craft large numbers of messages to persuade people based on their specific views.

The new Vanderbilt program has not found evidence of such hyper-targeted campaigns, but researchers said they were continuing to look.

item.title: Turning the Lens Around: Bob Woodward Takes On Bob Woodward
item.description:
He has interviewed presidents and kings and spies and generals. Along the way, he has extracted some of the most revelatory and enduring stories of the past half-century about the power players who run Washington. So what would Bob Woodward ask if he were interviewing Bob Woodward?

He was sitting in the sunroom of his Georgetown house on a bright autumn day when the question was put to him. He paused a moment before answering. “What is the internal turmoil?” he suggested. Which sounds like a good question. But what would his answer be? Mr. Woodward has long been more comfortable asking the questions than answering.

Perhaps the most renowned journalist of the modern age, Mr. Woodward has turned the lens on himself after 55 years of examining others, with a new memoir called “Secrets” recounting the story of his celebrated career. It may not exactly be a tell-all, but it is a tell-much and has already set Washington buzzing about the revelations it promises when it is published on Tuesday.

For the first time, he names names, disclosing the identities of many sources he has spent a career guarding, either because they have since died or because he obtained their permission. During Watergate, he reveals, some of his sources were President Richard M. Nixon’s own lawyers, who did not think much of their client. He divulges the names of five Supreme Court justices who talked for a book on the court. He identifies cabinet secretaries, White House aides and other officials who whispered secrets over the years.

For Mr. Woodward, the 83-year-old chronicler of modern Washington, this has all turned out to be a “liberating” experience. Not just because at long last he shows his homework, but because he has confronted, not always that willingly, his own story as well: how a boy from Wheaton, Ill., ended up at The Washington Post, found himself in an underground parking garage with a source nicknamed Deep Throat and changed history.

“I can tell the story. I don’t have to leave anything out,” Mr. Woodward said in a lengthy interview at the four-story, 19th-century home where he has hosted the prominent and powerful princelings of the nation’s capital. “Nothing is hidden here. Nothing is hidden. There’s not some story about some information I got from somebody. It’s all laid out there.”

Some of the most illuminating parts of the book hint at that “internal turmoil” he mentions. He writes about how at age 8 he began noticing troubles in his parents’ marriage and how at age 11 he discovered his mother kissing his father’s best friend. He learned that his parents were getting divorced by rifling through his father’s sock drawer where he found a letter mentioning it.

He writes about the fire that gutted the family home when he was a teenager and left him so frightened that to this day he keeps fire extinguishers stashed throughout his house — “at least a dozen,” according to his researcher Claire McMullen. He writes about how unnerved he was as a young Navy officer aboard a nuclear-armed ship with access to codes that could unleash Armageddon.

All of which taught him to be “a snoop” and “a catastrophic thinker,” as he puts it, to assume that there are always secrets and that the worst can happen. “I have lived since age 8 with suspicion about everything,” he said. And so a career was built. He would ferret out official secrets. He would explore worst-case scenarios. “In a way, it’s finding the sock drawer of history,” he said.

The process of writing a memoir after all these years had a predictably teeth-pulling quality to it for a man reluctant to talk about himself. The people closest to him kept pushing him to open up, including his wife, Elsa Walsh, herself an accomplished journalist; Carl Bernstein, the other half of the famed Watergate duo; and Scott Armstrong, his lifelong friend and former reporting partner.

“I said: ‘You’ve got to go deep. This is really the time to do it,’” Mr. Bernstein recalled. “‘The fabric of your life is incomplete unless you marry up both the deeply personal and the professional.’”

Ms. McMullen, a writer who has worked with Mr. Woodward on three previous books, made a point of recording their lunchtime conversations to try to get beyond all the interview memos he kept. The first time they sat down to talk about the memoir, she asked him a question he used to ask others: What was his first childhood memory?

She pored through many of the 500 boxes he has kept over the years containing not just memos of practically every interview of importance going back to the 1970s but other memorabilia and arcana collected over time. Nothing, it seems, was not saved. “Was this a historical sock,” she recalled asking of one discovery, “or just a sock?”

She took to relying on her own sources. “When I couldn’t get through to Bob on getting him to talk about something personal,” she said, “I’d call Carl and get him to tell me.”

Among the personal episodes recounted in the book is the rift between Mr. Woodward and Mr. Bernstein. When they followed up their book “All the President’s Men” with “The Final Days,” about the end of Nixon’s presidency, Mr. Woodward felt that Mr. Bernstein was not carrying his weight. (“It’s true,” Mr. Bernstein says now.) For a while, they stopped speaking.

When they finally made up, they concocted a “boy’s fairy tale” of an idea in which Mr. Woodward would take over as The Post’s Metro editor and Mr. Bernstein would become the Style editor. Then, when Benjamin C. Bradlee retired as executive editor, the two would run the newsroom together. When the idea made its way to the publisher, Katharine Graham, she is said to have quickly shot it down. “Are you out of your mind?” she reportedly exclaimed, adding that the two needed management, not the other way around.

Even so, there are limits to how much Mr. Woodward reveals. He is not by nature an introspective man, and some will undoubtedly finish the book wanting more. At some point, it becomes a recitation of all the important interviews he conducted with presidents and potentates, drawn often in great detail from the memos he kept. This is a record that historians will draw from for years to come, but it is not soul baring.

Mr. Woodward knows the criticism. He has heard it all before. He depends too much on anonymous sources. He has grown too close to power. He treats those who talk with him better than those who do not. He is not a particularly lyrical or analytical writer and does not put his inside-the-room reporting into context. A “stenographer to the rich and powerful,” as the writer Christopher Hitchens once acerbically put it.

To all of this now comes the latest criticism that in “Secrets” he finally identifies sources who have since died. While that has been his practice in the past, it has prompted a new debate about whether the promise of confidentiality survives death in the way that, say, attorney-client privilege does.

Donald E. Graham, the former publisher of The Post and Mrs. Graham’s son, came to Mr. Woodward’s defense recently against the negative reviews his books have received over the years. “They were being reviewed by journalists much less successful than Woodward and they reek of jealousy,” Mr. Graham wrote online.

“In the old days, they typically said, ‘How does Woodward dare to tell us all this astonishing stuff and not name his sources?’” Mr. Graham went on. “In this book, Bob DOES name several now-deceased people who were his sources over a lifetime. His reward is a review and many social-media comments asking how he can dare to name dead sources! Can’t win, I guess.”

Mr. Woodward, once played on the big screen by Robert Redford, concedes that he travels in more rarefied circles today than when he was a 20-something rookie investigating a rogue president. He has written about 11 presidents, interviewed 16 defense secretaries, runs into Supreme Court justices at parties and lives around the corner from cabinet officers.

He is, it is true, now part of the world he covers. But he argues that he uses that access to unearth information that would otherwise remain unknown. “Part of that world does not mean they set the terms,” he said. “I set the terms. And the terms are, I want to know what happened.”

Mr. Bernstein said Mr. Woodward had pulled secrets “out of the black hole of the modern presidency” that no one else could obtain and that have set a foundation for history. “People can argue over it, what the truth and the context is,” he said. “But it’s out there as information that never would have gotten out. And there is nothing comparable in the history of the country.”

That’s not to say Mr. Woodward has no regrets. With hindsight, he believes he missed the mark in “The Agenda,” his first book on President Bill Clinton, by overemphasizing the chaos of a White House that ultimately produced peace and prosperity. He acknowledges that he, like other reporters, was not skeptical enough about claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction before President George W. Bush’s invasion. He believes he did not take Covid-19 seriously enough at first.

But perhaps most of all, Mr. Woodward said, he wishes he had recognized the danger that he now believes President Trump poses and had done more before his first election in 2016 to explore what kind of president he would be. “I should have dropped everything and focused on Trump completely,” Mr. Woodward said.

The Trump presidency has been so extreme that it has propelled Mr. Woodward out of his traditional journalistic neutrality. In a new foreword to the 50th anniversary edition of “All the President’s Men” in 2022, he and Mr. Bernstein portrayed Mr. Trump as a greater threat to democracy than Nixon had been.

In the interview this month, Mr. Woodward, who has published five books about Mr. Trump, said the war against Iran demonstrated the danger. “Who starts wars?” he asked. “Tyrants start wars. It’s absolutely mind boggling, and it is a danger to the country.”

He traced his concerns about Mr. Trump to his own Navy days aboard a nuclear-armed ship. “I’m haunted by the danger we are in, having somebody in the presidency with that authority, unchecked, unmonitored,” he said. “It’s frightening. And I go back to that time as a 22-year-old seeing exactly how nuclear war can be started by a president.”

Mr. Woodward, the catastrophic thinker, added: “It keeps me up at night.” And he further added: “The impact of Trump is danger, danger, danger.”

All of which could lead to a little internal turmoil.

item.title: House Democrat Quits After Panel Alleges Unwanted Sexual Contact With Aide
item.description:
Representative Jimmy Gomez, Democrat of California, said on Monday that he would resign from Congress next week, after a House committee said it had found “substantial evidence” that he engaged in “unwelcome sexual conduct” with a female congressional aide.

In a report released on Monday afternoon, the bipartisan Ethics Committee said that it believed Mr. Gomez violated House rules that prohibit unwelcome sexual advances and sexual conduct toward employees, including with behavior that the panel said might have qualified as “criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”

In the report, the committee said that it had interviewed a woman who said that Mr. Gomez made two unwanted sexual advances on her while she was working in a House leadership office.

The woman, who is not identified in the report, said that on one occasion at a bar in Washington in February 2024, Mr. Gomez stuck his hand down her skirt and penetrated her with his fingers, an encounter she described as “nonconsensual,” according to the report. She said that Mr. Gomez was “forceful” months later when he tried to kiss her in his office on Capitol Hill.

Less than an hour after the committee released its report, Mr. Gomez, who lost his re-election bid this month and was set to leave office in early January, said in a statement that he had “strong disagreements with the committee’s report and its conclusions.”

But he said he recognized the “seriousness” of the panel’s findings and that he saw “no other alternative than to resign, effective Dec. 1.”

Mr. Gomez is the third lawmaker this year to resign in the face of sexual misconduct allegations. Both Representatives Eric Swalwell, Democrat of California, and Tony Gonzales, Republican of Texas, resigned in April after it became clear that the House might move to expel them. Both have denied wrongdoing.

And Representative Chuck Edwards, Republican of North Carolina, ended his re-election campaign after the Ethics Committee found that he “violated House rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.” Mr. Edwards has disputed the panel’s conclusions.

item.title: 2 City Bus Drivers Killed in Head-On Collision in Ohio
item.description:
Two bus drivers were killed and nine others were injured on Monday in a head-on collision between two city buses in Columbus, Ohio, officials said.

The crash occurred on the city’s north side, near Ohio State University and the Ohio State Fairgrounds, at about 8 a.m. when one bus apparently veered across a double-yellow line and collided with a bus heading in the opposite direction, according to the Columbus police. The bus that was hit was then rear-ended by a car.

The driver of the bus that had crossed the line died at the scene, the police said. The other driver was taken to a hospital in critical condition and was later pronounced dead. The Central Ohio Transportation Authority, which operates the buses, identified the drivers as Richard Terry, 53, and Paul Copeland, 60. The nine people who were injured were in stable condition at local hospitals, the police said.

Officials said it was not immediately clear what caused the bus to cut across its lane. A spokesman for COTA did not know which driver was driving each bus. Mr. Terry had been with COTA since 2012, while Mr. Copeland had joined the agency in 2008.

“We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of Richard and Paul, two valued members of our COTA family who dedicated their careers to serving our community,” Monica Tellez-Fowler, president of COTA, and Tyson Brown, president of Transportation Workers Union Local 208, said in a joint statement. “Richard and Paul were more than colleagues. They were friends, family members and valued members of Team COTA.”

Kerline Joseph, 49, who lives right by the site of the crash in one of the brick apartment buildings that house many students and employees at Ohio State University, was asleep on her sofa at the time of the accident.

“I heard a big bang and immediately ran to the back of the apartment because I’m always scared that there’s going to be a wreck and something is going to come through the front,” she said.

When Ms. Joseph went outside to see what had happened, she said, she saw bystanders yelling to call 911 and others rushing to help, including a doctor from Ohio State’s medical school.

Allissa Speaks, 28, a stay-at-home mother, said the crash “sounded like a bomb.” She looked out and saw two buses crumpled against each other, then raced out in her pajamas to see if she could help. She said she ran back inside to get a towel for a man who was bleeding from his forehead.

The Central Ohio Transit Authority operates public transportation in Columbus, the most populous city in the state. The agency, which runs nearly 40 bus routes that cover about 940 miles around the region, has expanded rapidly over the past decade, reflecting the growth around the state capital.

Shannon Hardin, president of the Columbus City Council, and Councilwoman Lourdes Barroso de Padilla called the deaths of the drivers “heartbreaking” in a joint statement, expressing sorrow for “the families that will be mourning them just as we enter the holiday season.”

item.title: More American Women Are Turning to Natural Family Planning, Study Shows
item.description:
For several years, social media has been awash in doubt about the birth control pill and other forms of hormonal contraception.

In its place, both the right and some on the left have embraced fertility awareness, also called natural family planning, in which women chart their menstrual cycles to determine the days when they will be fertile, allowing them to conceive or to prevent pregnancy.

Now, a new study has found that more women are using fertility awareness to avoid getting pregnant.

Reanalyzing previous survey data, researchers at the University of Utah and the Guttmacher Institute, which advocates for reproductive rights, found that between 2022 and 2023, more than 2.2 million American women aged 18 to 44 used a fertility-awareness-based method to prevent pregnancy — about 7 to 8 percent of the total number of women using some form of contraception.

That number roughly doubles an earlier finding from the National Survey of Family Growth, a government-run survey with data from 2013 to 2017.

Shifting trends in birth control have been hard to quantify because of changes in how national data has been collected in recent years. As a result, the old and new numbers should not be compared directly, the researchers cautioned, but the new findings still indicate an increase. In Idaho, Nevada and Utah, where an exact comparison is possible, fertility awareness use nearly doubled, to 14.5 percent, between 2022 and 2026.

“All lines of evidence really point to there being a true increase,” said Chelsea Polis, a research scientist at Guttmacher who led the study.

The rise in fertility-awareness-based methods does not necessarily mean a corresponding fall in hormonal birth control use. Instead, women adopting fertility awareness may not have been using any contraception before, or may have been using a nonhormonal strategy like condoms.

The researchers statistically analyzed data from four previous surveys, including the National Survey, this time including women who were using fertility awareness and another method for birth control, like condoms or withdrawal. Previously, they had been classified as using fertility awareness only if they were relying on that alone.

Religious conservatives have long supported fertility awareness and condemned hormonal birth control, which has long been celebrated as the key to women’s sexual and economic liberation.

But as distrust in conventional medicine has grown, more women have sought out information about hormones’ effects on their bodies. Some progressives have championed fertility awareness as a route to bodily empowerment, while devotees of the Make America Healthy Again movement and wellness influencers have encouraged cycle tracking as a way for women to connect naturally with their bodies — a rare point of convergence in the highly contested landscape of women’s reproductive health.

The study noted this wide support, finding that fertility-awareness-based methods grew across different religious affiliations. No one religion seemed to be driving its rise, though researchers have found that Christian women were using hormonal birth control less than before.

Other studies had also found that fertility awareness use was growing. In a nationally representative survey of reproductive-age women from KFF, a nonprofit that conducts health policy polling and research, 18 percent of contraceptive users relied on a fertility-awareness-based method this year, including women who were simultaneously using another method. That was up from 13 percent in 2024.

Data on the effectiveness of fertility awareness methods come mainly from small studies that are not considered high quality, said Dr. Polis, who is reviewing the research on fertility awareness’s effectiveness. The little existing data shows that two methods that require women to meticulously chart their cycles by measuring physical symptoms, the Marquette Method and Sensiplan, are comparable to the pill in efficacy. Other methods have an unintended pregnancy rate of 10 to 34 percent, roughly on par with condoms, sponges and diaphragms.

Also fueling the interest in fertility awareness are dozens of apps and other devices that are designed to track women’s menstrual cycles, part of a fast-growing, multibillion-dollar market for women’s health technology.

Allie Beth Stuckey, a prominent conservative Christian commentator and podcaster who has criticized hormonal birth control, recently released a cycle-tracking app, ana kate, which pairs information about women’s cycles with Bible verses and guidance for women who are pregnant, postpartum or trying to conceive.

Research has shown that many women interested in fertility awareness are tracking their cycles on such apps, which often rely on little more than the date of a woman’s last period to predict days of fertility — an approach considered far less effective than charting cycles based on symptoms such as urinary hormones and cervical mucus. Learning how to do so generally requires taking classes from an instructor.

Using calendar-based apps “is not a real way for them to prevent pregnancy,” said Rebecca Simmons, a University of Utah professor who coauthored a study in the Lancet, a British medical journal. “That’s the scary thing that keeps me up at night.”

Despite rising criticism, hormonal contraception — including the pill, intrauterine devices, implants, injections and patches, which all employ synthetic hormones to prevent ovulation or make it difficult for sperm to reach an egg — remains widely popular, according to Julia Strasser, a researcher at George Washington University who analyzed medical insurance claims data at the request of The New York Times.

Decades of research has shown the birth control pill to be safe and highly effective for most women, while also giving them far more control over their lives. And doctors have long urged women to use hormonal birth control, seeing it as the most effective option. But many health care providers and researchers worry that the pill is now falling victim to politically motivated smears and social media-fueled misinformation.

Hormonal birth control has also become more difficult to access in some places, said Dr. Simmons.

Some women may have lost Medicaid coverage under President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, making it harder for them to get hormonal contraception. In states including Idaho and Utah, family planning clinics have closed for lack of funding or no longer train clinicians in giving women implants or intrauterine devices.

The Trump administration is also asking family planning clinics applying for federal funding to prioritize expanding fertility awareness programs and helping women get pregnant instead of providing contraception.

But even mainstream health care providers are saying that fertility awareness should be taken seriously. Women who choose to use it because it fits their lifestyle, religious values or preferences need better data and resources, they say.

And in a field that has a history of pushing hormonal birth control more strongly on Black and poor women, clinicians should shift to prioritizing patients’ needs and desires over efficacy alone, said Dr. Polis, Dr. Simmons and several other researchers who were interviewed for this article.

“A lot of people are very frustrated by the lack of available options that are nonhormonal, and I think our field, the family planning field, has spent a long time not listening to that,” Dr. Simmons said, adding, “Many people are hungry to hear what their body is telling them, and fertility-awareness-based methods are a way to get a window into your own body.”

item.title: Trump Toasted a Troubled Boxer as a V.I.P. at Crypto Gala
item.description:
In his search for big names to help promote his memecoin at a gala on Sunday night, President Trump landed on Floyd Mayweather, a former world boxing champion.

He was a perplexing choice.

Until four days before the dinner, Mr. Mayweather faced two felony charges in Nevada stemming from a bad check, public records show. While that case was dismissed last Wednesday, records show that he still owes nearly $7.3 million in back federal taxes.

He is under court orders to pay $14 million to a luxury car dealer and more than $337,000 in back rent on a high-end Manhattan apartment. In 2011, he was convicted of a misdemeanor charge of battery in a domestic violence case and was sentenced to counseling and community service.

Mr. Trump has many connections in the sports world. So it is unclear how the president passed over baseball legends, N.F.L. superstars and even current world champion boxers to settle on Mr. Mayweather as a guest of honor at what was billed as “the most exclusive dinner in the world.” But it was not the first time he enlisted the boxer.

In mid-October, with the charges of theft and intent to defraud pending against him in a state court, Mr. Mayweather accompanied the president on Air Force One to a political rally in Bullhead City, Ariz.

Mr. Trump praised him there as “one of the greatest of all time.” He had “made probably more money than just about any fighter that I can imagine,” the president added. “In fact, his nickname is Money.”

Mr. Mayweather, his lawyer and his manager did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

The White House did not reply to questions about whether or how Mr. Mayweather was screened before either event and if so, how his legal troubles were viewed. Nor did the Trump Organization, whose subsidiary controlled the majority of memecoins issued.

The memecoin dinner was the third such sweepstakes in which Mr. Trump, a sitting president, offered access to himself to the top buyers of his digital token, prompting much criticism from Democrats. It was held at his golf club in Sterling, Va., a suburb of Washington.

In promoting the event, the sponsors said the dinner would feature “a private V.I.P. meet and greet” with Mr. Mayweather and two others: Kevin O’Leary, a star of the television series “Shark Tank,” and Tristan Thompson, an N.B.A. champion turned tech entrepreneur.

According to the rules of the dinner, for every coin that buyers purchased they received a point on a public leaderboard. The longer they held onto the tokens, the more points they accrued. The top 185 were invited to the event and the top 29 to a “V.I.P. reception” with Mr. Trump.

Mr. Mayweather, 49, was undefeated in his boxing career, with 50 wins before he left the arena about a decade ago. He is now trying to mount a comeback.

As the president noted at the political rally, he was also a prodigious moneymaker. In 2018, he topped Forbes’s annual list of the world’s highest-paid athletes for the fourth time in seven years. But he has a history of financial disputes over unpaid bills, money problems that appear to have escalated this year.

According to I.R.S. liens filed in March in Clark County, Nev., he owes more than $3 million for unpaid taxes in 2018 and $4.2 million for unpaid taxes in 2023. A review of records at that office on Monday indicated those debts are outstanding.

According to confidential documents reviewed by The New York Times, the I.R.S. has alerted the State Department not to renew Mr. Mayweather’s passport and this spring threatened to revoke it. ESPN has previously noted Mr. Mayweather’s passport issues.

His passport is apparently still good, though, because he recently traveled to Africa.

The felony charges, filed in April in Clark County, stemmed from a $200,000 purchase at Gold & Beyond, a high-end resale store in Las Vegas.

Prosecutors alleged that Mr. Mayweather knew the check he gave the store in December 2024 was bad. Mr. Mayweather’s lawyer said that the boxer had no intent to defraud the seller and that he would ultimately be vindicated.

The charges were dismissed on Nov. 18. That was two days after the memecoin gala organizers announced the “legends” who would appear with the president.

Adrian Lobo, a lawyer for Mr. Mayweather, said the charges were dropped after Mr. Mayweather returned an Audemars Piguet watch to the seller.

Pashtana Usufzy contributed reporting from Las Vegas. Susan C. Beachy contributed research.
